title: The siege of Gurdas Nangal, 1715
hookLine: starved in a mud fort for months, Banda's men are finally captured

lines: AN ARMY SETTLES IN TO WAIT.
cards: Mud walls. Not stone, not a fortress on a cliff. A walled compound in a village called Gurdas Nangal, with a ditch around it, and inside, Banda Singh and his people: fighters, and with them families.
Outside, an army settles in to wait. Nobody storms the walls. They don't need to.
They simply make sure nothing comes in: no grain, no supplies. Tradition says the waiting went on for months.

teach.h: A SIEGE FOUGHT WITH TIME AND HUNGER.
teach.b: A siege like this is fought with time and hunger. Sikh tellings describe what happened inside the walls as the food ran out.

People ate what grain was left, then the animals, then leaves and grass and the bark of trees. Some tellings go further, and they're hard to hear: people too weak to stand, still keeping their places.
Accounts differ on the very end, whether the gate was opened at last, or the army simply walked in on people who could no longer resist.
Either way, when hunger had done its work, Banda Singh and the men who were left were taken, worn to almost nothing. The line is they held on. Not they won.
Not they escaped. Sikhs have a word for this: sidak.
It means steadfastness, a faith that stays fixed when everything around it gives way. It isn't the same as courage in a charge. Courage can be a single moment.

Sidak is a long thing: what's left on yet another hungry morning, when nothing heroic is happening and nobody is watching. In Sikh memory, Gurdas Nangal is one of the places where that word was tested hardest.
There's a quieter lesson in it too, for a listener whose week has nothing to do with sieges.

teach.h: HOLDING ON OFTEN LOOKS LIKE NOTHING.
teach.b: Much of holding on looks like nothing.
It's not leaving. It's getting up again. It's staying where you said you'd stay.
That kind of faithfulness doesn't make a good painting, which is maybe why it's worth a word of its own.

how: Sikhs remember the siege of Gurdas Nangal, where Banda Singh Bahadur and his companions were starved until they were captured, as an example of sidak, steadfast faith.

o: a brave charge made in a single moment
the hunger that comes in a long siege
steadfast faith that stays fixed in hardship

games.q: inside the siege — tap the pairs.
p: a walled compound with a ditch

s: the army stormed the walls early on
in the tellings they waited, and let hunger do the work.
sidak is the same as a brave charge
sidak is long steadfastness, what's left on the hungry mornings.
Banda Singh was captured at Gurdas Nangal
when the people inside were too weak to resist.

games.q: you're inside the mud walls. the food is gone. nothing is coming in. what do the tellings say the people did?
o: opened the gates and gave up early.
ate leaves and bark and held their places.
games.why: Sikh tellings say they ate what they could find, down to leaves and bark, until they were captured.

practice: Notice your stomach right now: full, empty, somewhere between.
Then let your mind rest gently on people who are hungry today, near you or far away, who didn't choose it, and keep them company in your attention without pushing for a feeling.
After a while, come back to the people inside those mud walls and to the word sidak, and if you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Sidak, steadfastness. The long siege in which Banda Singh and his people were starved in a walled compound at Gurdas Nangal until they were captured.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sidak, steadfast faith that stays fixed in hardship.

carryVoice: Your line: they held on. Sidak is a long thing, not a single moment. Rest gently tonight.
